premises: A mass m on a linear spring of constant k, with a viscous damping force -b x', is driven by F0 cos(omega t). The equation of motion is written x'' + 2 beta x' + omega0^2 x = (F0/m) cos(omega t), with beta = b/(2m) and omega0^2 = k/m.
After the transients have decayed, the displacement is x = A cos(omega t - delta) with A = (F0/m) / sqrt((omega0^2 - omega^2)^2 + 4 beta^2 omega^2).
The damping is light enough that 2 beta^2 < omega0^2.
conclusion: The steady-state amplitude A is largest at the driving frequency omega_r given by omega_r^2 = omega0^2 - 2 beta^2, which lies below the natural frequency omega0.
source: Standard result (e.g. Marion & Thornton, Classical Dynamics, ch. 3): amplitude resonance of a damped driven oscillator.
explanation: Setting the derivative of (omega0^2 - omega^2)^2 + 4 beta^2 omega^2 with respect to omega^2 to zero gives omega^2 = omega0^2 - 2 beta^2, which is a genuine minimum of the denominator when 2 beta^2 < omega0^2.

premises: A mass m hangs from a linear spring of constant k in a uniform gravitational field g. The coordinate x is the extension of the spring beyond its unstretched length, positive downward, so Newton's law reads m x'' = -k x + m g.
Define the new coordinate y = x - m g/k, the displacement measured from the static equilibrium position.
conclusion: In the variable y the motion obeys y'' = -(k/m) y, so the hanging spring in gravity and the free horizontal mass-spring oscillator are the same oscillator; gravity only shifts the centre of oscillation and leaves the frequency unchanged.
source: Introductory mechanics texts (e.g. Halliday-Resnick-Walker, vertical spring-mass system).
explanation: Since y'' = x'' and -k x + m g = -k (x - m g/k) = -k y, the substitution is an exact change of variables that maps each description onto the other with no approximation.

premises: A damped oscillator m x'' + b x' + k x = F0 cos(omega t), with b > 0, has the steady-state solution x = A cos(omega t - delta), where A = (F0/m) / sqrt((omega0^2 - omega^2)^2 + 4 beta^2 omega^2), tan(delta) = 2 beta omega / (omega0^2 - omega^2), beta = b/(2m) and omega0^2 = k/m.
The driving frequency is now fixed at the natural frequency, omega = omega0.
conclusion: The steady-state amplitude reduces to A = F0/(b omega0), and the displacement lags the driving force by exactly a quarter of a period.
source: Special case of the general forced-oscillator solution; e.g. French, Vibrations and Waves, ch. 4.
explanation: Imposing omega = omega0 kills the first term in the square root, leaving A = (F0/m)/(2 beta omega0) = F0/(b omega0), and tan(delta) diverges with positive numerator so delta = pi/2; this is the general theory with one extra condition.

premises: For the driven oscillator x'' + 2 beta x' + omega0^2 x = (F0/m) cos(omega t), the steady-state amplitude is A(omega) = (F0/m) / sqrt((omega0^2 - omega^2)^2 + 4 beta^2 omega^2).
The exact maximum of A over omega occurs at omega_r^2 = omega0^2 - 2 beta^2 and equals A_max = (F0/m) / (2 beta sqrt(omega0^2 - beta^2)).
The oscillator is lightly damped: beta << omega0.
conclusion: In this regime the peak amplitude is A_max = F0/(2 m beta omega0), with a relative error of order beta^2/omega0^2.
source: Light-damping approximation to the resonance peak; e.g. Fowles & Cassiday, Analytical Mechanics.
explanation: Expanding 1/sqrt(omega0^2 - beta^2) = (1/omega0)(1 + beta^2/(2 omega0^2) + ...) shows the stated formula is the leading term with the stated error, valid precisely when beta << omega0.

premises: A weakly damped oscillator (beta << omega0) has displacement x(t) = A0 e^{-beta t} cos(omega_d t + phi), with omega_d^2 = omega0^2 - beta^2 and omega0^2 = k/m.
Its instantaneous mechanical energy is E = (1/2) m x'^2 + (1/2) k x^2, which fluctuates within each cycle because the damping force does work non-uniformly.
Denote by <E>(t) the energy averaged over one period 2 pi/omega_d of the fast oscillation, treating the slowly varying envelope e^{-beta t} as constant over that period.
conclusion: To leading order in beta/omega0 the cycle-averaged energy decays exponentially, <E>(t) = (1/2) k A0^2 e^{-2 beta t}.
source: Standard treatment of energy decay and Q in lightly damped oscillators; e.g. French, Vibrations and Waves, ch. 3.
explanation: Averaging cos^2 and sin^2 over a period each gives 1/2, and the cross terms of order beta/omega0 average to zero at leading order, so the fast intra-cycle fluctuations are removed and only the slow envelope e^{-2 beta t} remains.

premises: The underdamped oscillator x'' + 2 beta x' + omega0^2 x = 0 with beta < omega0 has solution x(t) = e^{-beta t} [C cos(omega_d t) + D sin(omega_d t)/omega_d], where omega_d = sqrt(omega0^2 - beta^2), C = x(0) and D = x'(0) + beta x(0).

Both cos(omega_d t) and sin(omega_d t)/omega_d are entire functions of omega_d^2, so the solution is an analytic function of the parameter omega_d^2 = omega0^2 - beta^2 and satisfies the differential equation identically in that parameter.
For beta > omega0 define gamma = sqrt(beta^2 - omega0^2), so that omega_d = i gamma.
conclusion: Continuing the parameter omega_d^2 to negative values gives the overdamped solution x(t) = e^{-beta t} [C cosh(gamma t) + D sinh(gamma t)/gamma] with the same C and D.
source: Unified treatment of under- and overdamped motion via cos(i z) = cosh(z); e.g. Symon, Mechanics, ch. 2.
explanation: Because the solution is analytic in omega_d^2 and the ODE holds identically, substituting omega_d = i gamma and using cos(i gamma t) = cosh(gamma t), sin(i gamma t)/(i gamma) = sinh(gamma t)/gamma gives a valid solution with the same initial data.

premises: A resistor R, inductor L and capacitor C are connected in parallel and fed by a current source I_s(t). Kirchhoff's current law for the common node voltage v(t), after one time derivative, is C v'' + (1/R) v' + (1/L) v = I_s'(t).
A driven mechanical oscillator obeys m x'' + b x' + k x = F(t), with quality factor Q = sqrt(k m)/b.

The two equations have identical mathematical form under the correspondence v <-> x, C <-> m, 1/R <-> b, 1/L <-> k, although voltage, capacitance and conductance are not displacement, mass and friction.
conclusion: Transcribing the mechanical quality factor through this correspondence, the parallel RLC circuit has Q = R sqrt(C/L), the reciprocal of the series-circuit expression, so a larger resistance means lighter damping in the parallel circuit.
source: Duality of series and parallel RLC circuits; e.g. Horowitz & Hill, The Art of Electronics, LC resonant circuits.
explanation: The substitution k -> 1/L, m -> C, b -> 1/R in sqrt(k m)/b gives R sqrt(C/L), which is the correct parallel-RLC quality factor; the claim only asserts a shared mathematical form, not a physical identity.

premises: A lossless LC circuit stores charge Q on the capacitor and magnetic flux Phi in the inductor. Its Hamiltonian is H = Q^2/(2C) + Phi^2/(2L), with Phi and Q a canonical pair, Poisson bracket {Phi, Q} = 1, so that Hamilton's equations reproduce dPhi/dt = Q/C and dQ/dt = -Phi/L.
The classical oscillation frequency is omega0 = 1/sqrt(LC).
The circuit is quantized by promoting Phi and Q to operators with the Poisson bracket replaced by the commutator [Phi, Q] = i hbar.
conclusion: The energy spectrum of the quantized circuit is E_n = hbar omega0 (n + 1/2), n = 0, 1, 2, ..., and the classical Hamiltonian is recovered as hbar -> 0.
source: Canonical quantization of the LC oscillator, the starting point of circuit QED (e.g. Devoret, Les Houches lectures 1995).
explanation: With Phi playing the role of coordinate and Q of momentum (or vice versa), H is a harmonic-oscillator Hamiltonian with mass C and stiffness 1/L (or mass L and stiffness 1/C), whose spectrum under [Phi, Q] = i hbar is hbar omega0 (n + 1/2).

premises: Two bodies slide without friction along a line. Each is attached to a fixed wall by a linear spring of constant k, and the two bodies are joined to each other by a linear spring of constant kappa. Let m denote the mass of the first body, and consider small oscillations.

The normal modes are the in-phase motion, in which both bodies move together and the coupling spring stays at its natural length, and the anti-phase motion, in which the midpoint of the coupling spring stays at rest and each body feels an extra restoring force 2 kappa times its displacement.
conclusion: The anti-phase normal mode has angular frequency given by omega_2^2 = (k + 2 kappa)/m.
source: Textbook two-mass coupled oscillator; common error of applying the symmetric-mode analysis to an unspecified (possibly asymmetric) system.
explanation: The in-phase/anti-phase mode structure and the resulting frequency hold only if the two masses are equal (and the wall springs equal); the premises never state that the second body also has mass m, and for m1 != m2 the modes are neither purely in-phase nor purely anti-phase.

premises: A series RLC circuit with L = 1.0 mH, C = 1.0 microfarad and R = 60 ohm is driven by an ideal source V0 cos(omega t). Writing omega0^2 = 1/(LC), the steady-state charge amplitude is q0 = (V0/L) / sqrt((omega0^2 - omega^2)^2 + (R omega/L)^2).
The capacitor voltage amplitude is V_C = q0/C, so V_C(omega) = V0 omega0^2 / sqrt((omega0^2 - omega^2)^2 + (R omega/L)^2).
Setting the derivative of the expression under the square root with respect to omega^2 to zero locates the extremum of V_C.
conclusion: The capacitor voltage is therefore maximal at a driving frequency somewhat below resonance, omega_max^2 = 1/(LC) - R^2/(2 L^2).
source: Capacitor-voltage resonance of the series RLC circuit; the formula is used outside its range R^2 < 2L/C (a frequent errata-type slip in worked examples).
explanation: With these values 2L/C = 2000 ohm^2 but R^2 = 3600 ohm^2, so the stationary point lies at negative omega^2 and does not exist; V_C decreases monotonically from its dc value and there is no peak, the formula holding only for R^2 < 2L/C.

premises: For a lightly damped oscillator written in the form x'' + gamma x' + omega0^2 x = 0, the stored energy decays as e^{-gamma t} and the quality factor is defined by Q = omega0/gamma.
The series RLC circuit obeys L q'' + R q' + q/C = 0 with omega0^2 = 1/(LC); its charge amplitude decays as e^{-R t/(2L)}, so the circuit's damping rate is gamma = R/(2L).
The circuit equation has the same form as the mechanical one, so the mechanical definition of Q may be carried over term by term.
conclusion: The quality factor of the series RLC circuit is Q = 2 omega0 L / R.
source: Classic factor-of-two error from mixing the 'gamma' convention (energy decay rate) with the 'beta' convention (amplitude decay rate); appears in student solutions and some errata lists.
explanation: In the gamma convention the coefficient of q' in q'' + (R/L) q' + q/(LC) = 0 gives gamma = R/L; the rate R/(2L) is the amplitude decay rate (beta = gamma/2) of a different convention, so combining them yields twice the correct value Q = omega0 L / R.

premises: A mass m on a spring of constant k with viscous damping -b x' is driven sinusoidally. In the steady state x = A cos(omega t - delta), and the average power dissipated by the damping force over one cycle is P = (1/2) b omega^2 A^2, where omega is the angular frequency appearing in x(t).
The oscillator's angular frequency satisfies omega^2 = k/m.
conclusion: Substituting the second relation into the first, the average dissipated power is P = b k A^2/(2 m), whatever the frequency at which the oscillator is driven.
source: Common student conflation of the driving frequency and the natural frequency, both written omega (Kleppner & Kolenkow-style problem sets).
explanation: The omega in the power formula is the driving frequency, while omega^2 = k/m defines the natural frequency omega0; the two coincide only at omega = omega0, so the result is not general and the argument conflates two quantities sharing one symbol.

premises: A capacitor C charged to q0 is connected at t = 0 through a switch to a series combination of an inductor L and resistor R, with R small enough that the discharge is oscillatory at angular frequency omega_d.
The product RC has the dimensions of time and is the characteristic time constant associated with a resistor and capacitor in a circuit.
The oscillating charge is confined within an exponentially decaying envelope whose time constant is fixed by the dissipative element R together with the energy-storing elements.
conclusion: The charge on the capacitor is q(t) = q0 e^{-t/(RC)} cos(omega_d t).
source: Student misconception: transplanting the RC time constant into the underdamped RLC envelope (seen in introductory E&M exams).
explanation: The envelope of the series RLC discharge is e^{-R t/(2L)}, with time constant 2L/R; RC is also a time but is a different physical quantity (the RC-only relaxation time), and equal units do not make it the RLC decay time.

premises: A simple pendulum obeys theta'' + omega0^2 sin(theta) = 0 with omega0^2 = g/L; it is released from rest at angle theta0.
For small angles sin(theta) = theta - theta^3/6 + ..., so the exact equation differs from the linearized equation theta'' + omega0^2 theta = 0 by terms of order theta0^3.
The linearized equation with the same initial conditions has the solution theta0 cos(omega0 t).
conclusion: Hence for small release angles the exact motion is theta(t) = theta0 cos(omega0 t) + O(theta0^3), the error bound holding uniformly for all t >= 0.
source: Secular-term issue in naive perturbation theory (Poincare-Lindstedt method motivation; Bender & Orszag ch. 11).
explanation: The cubic term shifts the frequency by about -omega0 theta0^2/16, so the phase error grows like theta0^2 omega0 t and the difference between exact and linear solutions becomes of order theta0 (not theta0^3) after times of order 1/(omega0 theta0^2); the small-angle limit and the long-time limit do not commute.

premises: Any one-dimensional motion satisfying x'' = -omega^2 x, with omega > 0, is periodic: the system returns to the same position and velocity after every interval T = 2 pi/omega.
A mechanical oscillator is observed with a stopwatch to return exactly to its initial position and velocity after every interval of T seconds.
conclusion: The oscillator's displacement therefore obeys x'' = -(2 pi/T)^2 x.
source: Misconception that 'periodic' means 'simple harmonic' (documented in physics-education studies on oscillation concepts).
explanation: The implication runs only from the linear equation to periodicity; periodic motion need not be harmonic (a large-amplitude pendulum or any anharmonic potential well gives periodic non-sinusoidal motion), so the converse asserted here does not hold.

premises: The series RLC equation L q'' + R q' + q/C = V(t) and the mechanical equation m x'' + b x' + k x = F(t) are identical in form under q <-> x, L <-> m, R <-> b, 1/C <-> k, V <-> F.

In the mechanical system m is the inertia of the moving body and (1/2) m v^2 is the kinetic energy of that body; correspondingly the inductor's energy (1/2) L I^2 is the energy associated with the moving charge.
The current in the coil's wire, of length l, cross-section A and conduction-electron density n, is I = n e A v_d, carried by N = n A l electrons of mass m_e moving at drift velocity v_d.
conclusion: Identifying (1/2) L I^2 with the electrons' kinetic energy (1/2) N m_e v_d^2 gives the coil's inductance as L = m_e l/(n e^2 A).
source: Misconception that inductance is the 'inertia of electrons'; the expression is the (usually negligible) kinetic inductance, not the magnetic inductance of a coil.
explanation: The mechanical-electrical correspondence is only a shared equation form; the coil's inductance is set by the magnetic-field energy (1/2) L I^2 stored in the field, and treating the analogy as a physical identity between mass and electron mass yields a value many orders of magnitude too small for an ordinary coil.

premises: A mass m on a spring of constant k moves along a line under a viscous drag force -b dx/dt, so that m d^2x/dt^2 + b dx/dt + k x = 0 with b, k, m > 0 in SI units.
The damping is subcritical, b^2 < 4 m k. Write gamma = b/(2m) and omega_d = sqrt(k/m - gamma^2).
x_n denotes the value of x at its n-th successive local maximum, n = 1, 2, 3, ...
conclusion: ln(x_n / x_(n+1)) = 2 pi gamma / omega_d
source: Logarithmic decrement; standard result in French, Vibrations and Waves, and in engineering vibration texts.
explanation: The general solution is x = A e^(-gamma t) cos(omega_d t + phi); its maxima occur where tan(omega_d t + phi) = -gamma/omega_d, which repeats exactly every 2 pi/omega_d, so successive maxima are in the exact ratio e^(2 pi gamma/omega_d).

premises: x(t) satisfies d^2x/dt^2 + 2 gamma dx/dt + omega0^2 x = 0, where gamma >= 0 and omega0 > 0 are constants (any ratio gamma/omega0 is allowed).
Define the new dependent variable y(t) = e^(gamma t) x(t), so that x(t) = e^(-gamma t) y(t).
conclusion: d^2y/dt^2 + (omega0^2 - gamma^2) y = 0
source: Standard substitution that removes the first-derivative term; e.g. Marion and Thornton, Classical Dynamics, damped oscillations.
explanation: Substituting x = e^(-gamma t) y cancels the first-derivative term identically, and the map x <-> y is invertible for all t, so the two equations describe the same motion for every value of gamma, with y harmonic, linear, or hyperbolic according to the sign of omega0^2 - gamma^2.

premises: Two equal masses m slide without friction on a line. Each mass is joined to a fixed wall by a spring of constant k, and the two masses are joined to each other by a spring of constant kappa. x1 and x2 are the displacements from equilibrium, measured positive in the same direction.
The equations of motion are m d^2x1/dt^2 = -k x1 - kappa (x1 - x2) and m d^2x2/dt^2 = -k x2 - kappa (x2 - x1).
Impose the initial condition x1(0) = A, x2(0) = -A, dx1/dt(0) = dx2/dt(0) = 0.
conclusion: x1(t) = A cos( sqrt((k + 2 kappa)/m) t )
source: Antisymmetric normal mode of two coupled masses; any intermediate mechanics text.
explanation: With these initial data the ansatz x2 = -x1 satisfies both equations and the initial conditions, so by uniqueness it is the motion; the first equation then reduces to m x1'' = -(k + 2 kappa) x1, a single oscillator, which is the general theory with the extra condition x1 = -x2 imposed.

premises: The steady state of m d^2x/dt^2 + b dx/dt + k x = F0 cos(omega t) has amplitude A(omega) = (F0/m) / sqrt((omega0^2 - omega^2)^2 + (2 gamma omega)^2), where omega0 = sqrt(k/m) and gamma = b/(2m).
The damping is weak, gamma << omega0, and the driving frequency lies in the band |omega - omega0| << omega0.
conclusion: Within this band, with relative error of order |omega - omega0| / omega0, A(omega) = (F0 / (2 m omega0)) / sqrt((omega - omega0)^2 + gamma^2)
source: Lorentzian (resonance) approximation to the driven oscillator; e.g. Feynman Lectures Vol. I ch. 23.
explanation: Writing omega0^2 - omega^2 = (omega0 - omega)(omega0 + omega) and replacing omega0 + omega by 2 omega0 and 2 gamma omega by 2 gamma omega0 introduces relative errors of order |omega - omega0|/omega0 in each term, giving the stated Lorentzian in the stated regime.

premises: Two identical pendulums (bob mass m, length l, omega0 = sqrt(g/l)) swing at small angles in the same plane; their bobs are joined by a weak spring of constant kappa with kappa/(m omega0^2) << 1.
The normal modes are the in-phase mode with angular frequency omega_+ = omega0 and the anti-phase mode with omega_- = sqrt(omega0^2 + 2 kappa/m); define Delta = omega_- - omega_+.
At t = 0 pendulum 1 is released from rest with displacement A and pendulum 2 is at rest at its equilibrium position.
E1(t) denotes the kinetic plus gravitational potential energy of pendulum 1 averaged over one period 2 pi/omega0 of the fast oscillation, and E0 = (1/2) m omega0^2 A^2 is the initial energy.
conclusion: E1(t) = E0 cos^2(Delta t / 2)
source: Beats and energy exchange between weakly coupled pendulums; French, Vibrations and Waves ch. 5; Crawford, Waves.
explanation: The exact motion is x1 = A cos(Delta t/2) cos((omega_+ + omega_-) t/2); averaging the energy over the fast period while the slow envelope cos(Delta t/2) is essentially constant gives E1 = E0 cos^2(Delta t/2) up to corrections of relative order kappa/(m omega0^2), which is the averaged, large-scale description of the beats.

premises: For d^2x/dt^2 + 2 gamma dx/dt + omega0^2 x = 0 with 0 < gamma < omega0, the solution with x(0) = A and dx/dt(0) = B - gamma A is x(t) = e^(-gamma t) [ A cos(omega_d t) + B sin(omega_d t) / omega_d ], where omega_d = sqrt(omega0^2 - gamma^2).
Now let gamma > omega0 and define kappa = sqrt(gamma^2 - omega0^2) > 0, so that omega_d is continued to the imaginary value omega_d = i kappa, using cos(i u) = cosh(u) and sin(i u) = i sinh(u).
conclusion: x(t) = e^(-gamma t) [ A cosh(kappa t) + B sinh(kappa t) / kappa ]
source: Underdamped-to-overdamped continuation; e.g. Taylor, Classical Mechanics sec. 5.4, and Morin.
explanation: The bracket is an entire function of omega_d^2 (cos(omega_d t) and sin(omega_d t)/omega_d are even in omega_d), so continuation to omega_d^2 < 0 is unambiguous and yields exactly the overdamped solution with the same initial data.

premises: A chain of equal masses m on a line, each joined to its two neighbours by springs of constant K with lattice spacing a, obeys m d^2u_n/dt^2 = K (u_(n+1) - 2 u_n + u_(n-1)) for small displacements u_n, and has travelling-wave solutions u_n = U exp(i(q n a - omega t)) with dispersion relation omega = 2 sqrt(K/m) |sin(q a / 2)|.

A ladder network consists of identical series inductors L between successive nodes, each node connected to ground through a capacitor C, with a nominal cell length a. By Kirchhoff's laws the node charge q_n obeys L d^2q_n/dt^2 = (q_(n+1) - 2 q_n + q_(n-1)) / C, which has the same form as the chain equation under the correspondence m -> L, K -> 1/C, u_n -> q_n.
conclusion: omega = (2 / sqrt(L C)) |sin(q a / 2)|
source: Mechanical chain versus LC transmission-line ladder; Crawford, Waves (Berkeley Physics Course vol. 3) ch. 2-4.
explanation: The two difference equations are identical in form, so the dispersion relation carries over under the stated substitution; the physics (displacements of masses versus charges on capacitors) is different, and nothing beyond the shared mathematics is claimed.

premises: An ideal LC circuit (no resistance) has energy H = q^2/(2C) + Phi^2/(2L), where q is the capacitor charge and Phi = L I is the flux linkage of the inductor; Hamilton's equations with q as coordinate and Phi as conjugate momentum reproduce dq/dt = I and L dI/dt = -q/C.
The circuit is quantized canonically by promoting q and Phi to operators with [q, Phi] = i hbar, and E_n (n = 0, 1, 2, ...) denote the energy eigenvalues of the resulting Hamiltonian.
conclusion: E_n = hbar (n + 1/2) / sqrt(L C)
source: Quantum LC oscillator, the starting point of circuit QED; e.g. Devoret's Les Houches lectures on quantum fluctuations in electrical circuits.
explanation: The Hamiltonian is a harmonic oscillator with 'mass' L and 'spring constant' 1/C, so the canonical quantization with [q, Phi] = i hbar gives the standard spectrum hbar omega (n + 1/2) with omega = 1/sqrt(LC), the quantum deformation of the classical circuit.

premises: A particle of mass m moves in one dimension in a smooth potential U(x) with a single minimum at x = 0, where U'(0) = 0 and U''(0) = k > 0.
The particle is released from rest at x = A > 0 and oscillates about x = 0; T denotes the period of this oscillation.
conclusion: T = 2 pi sqrt(m / k)
source: Common student error: treating every oscillation about a potential minimum as isochronous; cf. Landau and Lifshitz Mechanics sec. 11 on the amplitude dependence of the period.
explanation: The period equals 2 pi sqrt(m/k) only if the amplitude is small enough that the cubic and higher terms of U are negligible (or U is exactly quadratic); the premises say nothing about the size of A or the higher derivatives of U, so the needed assumption is missing.

premises: For m d^2x/dt^2 + b dx/dt + k x = 0 define omega0 = sqrt(k/m), the quality factor Q = m omega0 / b, and omega_d as the angular frequency of the damped oscillation.
For Q >> 1 the damped frequency is given by omega_d = omega0 (1 - 1/(8 Q^2)), with relative error of order Q^(-4).
Consider the oscillator with b = 2 sqrt(k m), that is Q = 1/2.
conclusion: omega_d = omega0 / 2
source: Misuse of the large-Q expansion of omega_d = omega0 sqrt(1 - 1/(4 Q^2)); recurring homework error.
explanation: The expansion of sqrt(1 - 1/(4Q^2)) holds only for Q >> 1; at Q = 1/2 the oscillator is critically damped and omega_d = 0, so the formula is applied outside the parameter range in which it is valid.

premises: The free damped oscillator d^2x/dt^2 + 2 gamma dx/dt + omega0^2 x = 0 with 0 < gamma < omega0 has solutions whose amplitude decays as exp(-gamma t), and the energy E is proportional to the square of the amplitude.
For a lightly damped oscillator the quality factor is Q = omega0 / gamma, where gamma is the damping constant of the oscillator.
E0 denotes the energy at t = 0.
conclusion: E(t) = E0 exp(-2 omega0 t / Q)
source: Factor-of-two mismatch between texts writing 2 gamma x' (Taylor, Q = omega0/(2 gamma)) and texts writing gamma x' (French, Q = omega0/gamma).
explanation: The relation Q = omega0/gamma belongs to the convention x'' + gamma x' + omega0^2 x = 0 in which gamma is the energy decay rate; in the stated equation the damping constant is 2 gamma and Q = omega0/(2 gamma), so the correct result is E = E0 exp(-omega0 t/Q).

premises: A driven damped oscillator obeys m d^2x/dt^2 + b dx/dt + k x = F0 cos(omega t), and its steady-state motion is x(t) = A cos(omega t - phi) with tan(phi) = b omega / (k - m omega^2), where 0 <= phi <= pi.
The oscillator's angular frequency is omega = sqrt(k/m), so that k - m omega^2 = 0.
conclusion: phi = pi / 2
source: Student misconception that a driven oscillator vibrates at its own natural frequency; conflation of driving and natural frequency symbols.
explanation: The symbol omega denotes the driving frequency in the first premise and the natural frequency in the second; the steady state runs at the driving frequency, which is arbitrary, and phi = pi/2 holds only in the special case omega = sqrt(k/m).

premises: A series RLC circuit obeys L d^2q/dt^2 + R dq/dt + q/C = 0. Its free response changes from oscillatory to non-oscillatory at a critical resistance R_c that depends only on L and C.

The only combination of L and C with the SI units of resistance (ohm) is sqrt(L/C), the characteristic impedance of the circuit; the transition to non-oscillatory behaviour occurs when the resistance matches this impedance.
conclusion: R_c = sqrt(L / C)
source: Confusion between characteristic impedance sqrt(L/C) and the critical-damping resistance 2 sqrt(L/C); a recurring erratum in circuit problem solutions.
explanation: Sharing the unit ohm does not make the characteristic impedance the same quantity as the critical resistance; solving R^2 = 4L/C for critical damping gives R_c = 2 sqrt(L/C).

premises: For m d^2x/dt^2 + b dx/dt + k x = F0 cos(omega t) with b > 0, every solution approaches the steady state x_s(t) = A(omega) cos(omega t - phi) as t -> infinity, with A(omega) = (F0/m) / sqrt((omega0^2 - omega^2)^2 + (b omega/m)^2) and omega0 = sqrt(k/m).
For fixed omega != omega0, as b -> 0 the steady state tends to x_s(t) = F0 cos(omega t) / (m (omega0^2 - omega^2)), since A -> F0/(m |omega0^2 - omega^2|) and phi -> 0 or pi.
Consider the undamped oscillator b = 0 driven at omega != omega0 and starting from rest at x = 0.
conclusion: lim_(t -> infinity) [ x(t) - F0 cos(omega t) / (m (omega0^2 - omega^2)) ] = 0
source: Interchange of the limits t -> infinity and b -> 0 for the driven oscillator; the undamped solution (cos(omega t) - cos(omega0 t)) never loses its transient.
explanation: The transient decays on the time scale 2m/b, which diverges as b -> 0, so the limits do not commute; for b = 0 the solution is [F0/(m(omega0^2 - omega^2))](cos(omega t) - cos(omega0 t)), which beats forever and has no limit.

premises: For the weakly damped oscillator m d^2x/dt^2 + b dx/dt + k x = 0 with b << sqrt(k m), the energy E = (1/2) m (dx/dt)^2 + (1/2) k x^2 averaged over one cycle, <E>, obeys d<E>/dt = -(b/m) <E>, so that <E>(t) = E0 exp(-b t/m).
Because the cycle average commutes with d/dt and the exponential law for <E> holds at every instant t, the same first-order law governs the unaveraged energy E(t).
conclusion: dE/dt = -(b/m) E
source: Reversal of the cycle-averaging step in the standard Q derivation; cf. French, Vibrations and Waves, and common exam errors.
explanation: Exactly, dE/dt = -b (dx/dt)^2, which vanishes at the turning points and equals -2(b/m)E at the equilibrium crossings; the averaged decay law is a one-way consequence and cannot be run backwards to the instantaneous energy.

premises: Two identical pendulums (mass m, omega0 = sqrt(g/l)) coupled by a weak spring of constant kappa, with pendulum 1 initially excited, exchange energy so that the fraction in pendulum 2 averaged over the fast oscillation is E2/E0 = sin^2(Delta t / 2), where Delta = omega_- - omega_+ = kappa / (m omega0) to first order in kappa/(m omega0^2).

A two-level atom initially in its ground state and driven resonantly by a classical field has excited-state probability P_e(t) = sin^2(Omega_R t / 2), where Omega_R is the Rabi frequency (optical Bloch equations in the rotating-wave approximation).

Both systems are governed by the same pair of coupled first-order equations for two slowly varying amplitudes, so the coupled pendulums are a two-level quantum system whose Rabi frequency is set by the spring coupling.
conclusion: Omega_R = kappa / (m omega0)
source: Popular 'classical Rabi oscillation' demonstrations with coupled pendulums, sometimes overstated as an equivalence rather than an analogy.
explanation: The slow-envelope equations share a mathematical form, but classical energy fractions are not quantum probability amplitudes and the pendulums have no two-level Hilbert space; the analogy is promoted to a physical identity, and the equation merely relabels the beat frequency as a Rabi frequency.

premises: A particle on a line moves with constant speed v and reverses direction at the events of a Poisson process of rate lambda (reversals are independent of position and of past history).
Let p_+(x,t) and p_-(x,t) be the probability densities of right-moving and left-moving particles. They obey dp_+/dt + v dp_+/dx = lambda (p_- - p_+) and dp_-/dt - v dp_-/dx = lambda (p_+ - p_-).
The total density is p = p_+ + p_- and the current is j = v (p_+ - p_-).
conclusion: The total density satisfies the telegraph equation d^2p/dt^2 + 2 lambda dp/dt = v^2 d^2p/dx^2.
source: Goldstein (1951) and Kac (1974), persistent random walk and the telegraph equation.
explanation: Adding the two transport equations gives continuity dp/dt + dj/dx = 0, subtracting gives dj/dt + v^2 dp/dx = -2 lambda j; eliminating j by one more time derivative yields exactly the stated telegraph equation.

premises: A passive scalar u(x,t) in a uniform flow of velocity v along x obeys the advection-diffusion equation du/dt + v du/dx = D d^2u/dx^2 on the whole real line, with D a constant.
Define the co-moving coordinate xi = x - v t and the function w(xi,t) = u(xi + v t, t).
conclusion: u solves the advection-diffusion equation if and only if w solves the pure diffusion equation dw/dt = D d^2w/dxi^2.
source: Standard Galilean invariance of the advection-diffusion equation (e.g. Crank, The Mathematics of Diffusion).
explanation: With u(x,t) = w(x - v t, t) the chain rule gives du/dt + v du/dx = dw/dt and d^2u/dx^2 = d^2w/dxi^2, so the two equations map onto each other exactly and invertibly.

premises: An overdamped Brownian particle in a potential U(x) obeys the Langevin equation gamma dx/dt = -U'(x) + xi(t), with gamma the friction coefficient in kg/s and Gaussian white noise <xi(t) xi(t')> = 2 gamma k_B T delta(t - t').
Its probability density obeys the Smoluchowski equation dp/dt = d/dx[ (U'(x)/gamma) p ] + D d^2p/dx^2 with D = k_B T/gamma.
The potential is now taken to be harmonic, U(x) = (1/2) kappa x^2, with kappa > 0.
conclusion: The density obeys dp/dt = (kappa/gamma) d(x p)/dx + D d^2p/dx^2.
source: Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process as the harmonic special case of the Smoluchowski equation (Risken, The Fokker-Planck Equation).
explanation: Substituting U'(x) = kappa x into the general Smoluchowski equation gives the stated equation directly; nothing beyond the extra condition on U is used.

premises: A particle on a one-dimensional lattice of spacing a jumps to each neighbouring site with rate nu/2 (total jump rate nu), the waiting times being exponential and independent.
The occupation probability obeys the master equation dp_n/dt = (nu/2)(p_{n+1} + p_{n-1} - 2 p_n).
The probability is smooth on a length scale L, in the sense that p_n = p(n a, t) with p having bounded derivatives and a << L.
conclusion: Expanding p(x +/- a) in a Taylor series, the master equation becomes dp/dt = D d^2p/dx^2 with D = nu a^2/2, the neglected term (D a^2/12) d^4p/dx^4 being of relative size O(a^2/L^2).
source: Kramers-Moyal expansion of the simple random walk master equation (van Kampen, Stochastic Processes in Physics and Chemistry).
explanation: The Taylor expansion of p(x+a) + p(x-a) - 2p(x) gives a^2 p'' + (a^4/12) p'''' + O(a^6), so the diffusion equation is the leading term with the stated correction and regime.

premises: A solute of molecular diffusivity D is carried by steady laminar Poiseuille flow u(r) = 2U(1 - r^2/a^2) in a straight circular tube of radius a, U being the cross-sectionally averaged speed.
The concentration obeys dc/dt + u(r) dc/dz = D ( (1/r) d/dr (r dc/dr) + d^2c/dz^2 ) with zero radial flux at the wall r = a.

Times considered satisfy t >> a^2/D, so the solute has sampled the whole cross-section many times, and the cross-sectionally averaged concentration C(z,t) = (2/a^2) integral_0^a c r dr varies slowly along z.
conclusion: The averaged concentration obeys the one-dimensional advection-diffusion equation dC/dt + U dC/dz = D_eff d^2C/dz^2 with D_eff = D + a^2 U^2/(48 D).
source: Taylor (1953) and Aris (1956), shear dispersion in a tube.
explanation: Averaging over the cross-section after the radial profile has relaxed produces an effective axial diffusivity; the Taylor-Aris coefficient a^2 U^2/(48 D) plus molecular D is the exact long-time result for this geometry.

premises: For real D > 0 the fundamental solution of du/dt = D d^2u/dx^2 with u(x,0) = delta(x) is G(x,t) = (4 pi D t)^(-1/2) exp(-x^2/(4 D t)) for t > 0.
The free Schroedinger equation i hbar dpsi/dt = -(hbar^2/2m) d^2psi/dx^2 can be written dpsi/dt = D_q d^2psi/dx^2 with D_q = i hbar/(2m).
The expression for G is continued in D from the positive real axis to D_q along a path in the right half-plane, the square root being taken on the branch that is continuous along this path.
conclusion: The free-particle propagator is K(x,t) = (m/(2 pi i hbar t))^(1/2) exp(i m x^2/(2 hbar t)).
source: Feynman and Hibbs, free-particle kernel via Wick rotation of the heat kernel.
explanation: Setting D = i hbar/(2m) in (4 pi D t)^(-1/2) exp(-x^2/(4 D t)) gives exactly the stated kernel, and the continued function solves the Schroedinger equation with delta initial data because the PDE is linear in D.

premises: A submarine cable has series resistance r per unit length and shunt capacitance c per unit length; series inductance and shunt leakage conductance are negligible.
Kirchhoff's laws for a line element give dV/dx = -r I and dI/dx = -c dV/dt, where V(x,t) is the voltage to ground and I(x,t) the series current.
conclusion: The voltage obeys dV/dt = (1/(r c)) d^2V/dx^2, which has the same mathematical form as the one-dimensional heat equation with diffusivity 1/(r c), although V is a potential rather than a conserved density and no random motion of charge carriers is implied.
source: Kelvin (1855), the RC cable equation and Fourier's theory of heat.
explanation: Eliminating I gives a parabolic equation identical in form to Fourier's equation; the analogy is purely mathematical since the physical quantities and mechanisms differ.

premises: A quantum particle of mass m in a potential U(x), coupled to an Ohmic bath at temperature T with k_B T >> hbar gamma, has a Wigner function obeying the Caldeira-Leggett master equation dW/dt = -(p/m) dW/dx + U'(x) dW/dp - (hbar^2/24) U'''(x) d^3W/dp^3 + O(hbar^4) + gamma d(p W)/dp + gamma m k_B T d^2W/dp^2, where gamma is the momentum damping rate in 1/s.
The classical limit is taken as hbar -> 0 with m, T, gamma and U fixed, the Wigner function remaining smooth in p on scales set by m k_B T.
conclusion: In this limit W obeys the classical Kramers equation dW/dt = -(p/m) dW/dx + U'(x) dW/dp + gamma d(p W)/dp + gamma m k_B T d^2W/dp^2.
source: Caldeira and Leggett (1983); classical limit of the quantum Brownian motion master equation in Wigner representation.
explanation: The Moyal correction terms carry explicit powers of hbar^2 and vanish as hbar -> 0 under the stated smoothness, leaving the classical phase-space Fokker-Planck (Kramers) equation of which the quantum equation is the deformation.

premises: Fick's first law states that the diffusive flux of a solute is proportional to the negative concentration gradient, J = -D dc/dx, where D is the diffusion coefficient of the solute in the given solvent.
Conservation of solute gives the continuity equation dc/dt + dJ/dx = 0.
conclusion: Combining the two laws gives Fick's second law dc/dt = D d^2c/dx^2.
source: Common textbook shortcut; Crank notes that the form dc/dt = D d^2c/dx^2 requires D independent of concentration and position.
explanation: Substituting J into the continuity equation gives dc/dt = d/dx(D dc/dx); pulling D outside the derivative requires the unstated assumption that D does not depend on x or on c, which fails for concentration-dependent or inhomogeneous diffusion.

premises: A Brownian sphere of radius a in a fluid of viscosity eta is described by the overdamped Langevin equation 6 pi eta a dx/dt = xi(t) with <xi(t) xi(t')> = 2 (6 pi eta a) k_B T delta(t - t'), which gives <Delta x^2(t)> = 2 D t with D = k_B T/(6 pi eta a) for all t > 0.
A silica bead has a = 0.5e-6 m and density 2000 kg/m^3; it is suspended in water with eta = 1.0e-3 Pa s at T = 300 K, so D = 4.4e-13 m^2/s.
The bead's position is sampled with a time resolution of 1 ns.
conclusion: Over one sampling interval the mean-square displacement along x is <Delta x^2(1 ns)> = 2 D t = 8.8e-22 m^2.
source: Misapplication of the overdamped limit; see Li et al. (2010) on the ballistic regime of Brownian motion.
explanation: The overdamped model holds only for t >> m/(6 pi eta a), which for this bead is about 1.1e-7 s; at 1 ns the motion is ballistic with <Delta x^2> = (k_B T/m) t^2 of order 4e-24 m^2, so the formula is used far outside its regime.

premises: Einstein's 1905 result for a Brownian particle is <Delta x^2(t)> = 2 D t, the mean-square displacement along a single coordinate axis over a time t.
The Stokes-Einstein relation gives D = k_B T/(6 pi eta a) for a sphere of radius a in a fluid of viscosity eta.
In a three-dimensional single-particle tracking experiment the quantity recorded is the full squared displacement |Delta r|^2 = Delta x^2 + Delta y^2 + Delta z^2, averaged over many trajectories.
conclusion: The recorded mean-square displacement grows as <|Delta r|^2(t)> = k_B T t/(3 pi eta a).
source: Known factor-of-d error in particle-tracking analyses when 1D and 3D MSD normalizations are mixed (see e.g. Qian, Sheetz and Elson 1991).
explanation: The premise 2 D t is the one-axis normalization; the isotropic three-dimensional displacement is the sum of three such contributions, <|Delta r|^2> = 6 D t = k_B T t/(pi eta a), so the conclusion is low by a factor of three.

premises: A Brownian particle of mass m obeys m dv/dt = -gamma v + xi(t), where gamma = 6 pi eta a is the Stokes friction coefficient and <xi(t) xi(t')> = 2 gamma k_B T delta(t - t').
The velocity is an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process whose autocorrelation decays exponentially, <v(0) v(t)> = <v^2> exp(-gamma t), with <v^2> = k_B T/m by equipartition.
The Green-Kubo formula gives the diffusion coefficient as D = integral_0^infinity <v(0) v(t)> dt.
conclusion: Evaluating the integral gives D = k_B T/(m gamma).
source: Widespread student error from using gamma both for the friction coefficient (kg/s) and for the velocity relaxation rate (1/s); noted in errata to several statistical mechanics texts.
explanation: In the second premise the decay rate must be gamma/m, not gamma, when gamma denotes the friction coefficient; carrying the same symbol through gives D = k_B T/(m gamma) instead of the correct D = k_B T/gamma.

premises: When a flat plate bounding a fluid at rest is impulsively set in motion, the fluid velocity obeys du/dt = nu d^2u/dy^2 with nu = eta/rho, and vorticity has penetrated a distance delta_v(t) = 2 (nu t)^(1/2) after time t.
When the same plate is instead suddenly heated, the fluid temperature obeys dT/dt = alpha d^2T/dy^2 with alpha = k/(rho c_p).
Both nu and alpha are diffusivities measured in m^2/s, and the two governing equations are identical in form.
conclusion: The thermal penetration depth therefore equals the viscous one, delta_T(t) = 2 (nu t)^(1/2).
source: Misconception that equal units imply equal transport rates; the ratio nu/alpha is the Prandtl number (Pr = 7 for water, 0.7 for air).
explanation: Kinematic viscosity and thermal diffusivity share units and governing equation but are distinct material properties; the thermal depth is 2 (alpha t)^(1/2), which differs from the viscous depth by the factor Pr^(-1/2).

premises: The Goldstein-Kac density obeys d^2p/dt^2 + 2 lambda dp/dt = v^2 d^2p/dx^2 with p(x,0) = delta(x) and dp/dt(x,0) = 0.
In the diffusion limit lambda -> infinity, v -> infinity with D = v^2/(2 lambda) fixed, p(x,t) converges for each fixed x and t to G(x,t) = (4 pi D t)^(-1/2) exp(-x^2/(4 D t)).
For finite but large lambda the diffusion limit is approached once t >> 1/lambda.
conclusion: For t >> 1/lambda the telegraph solution is described by the Gaussian throughout space, p(x,t) = G(x,t) (1 + O(1/(lambda t))) for all x.
source: Known subtlety of the telegraph-to-diffusion limit (Kac 1974; Weiss, Aspects and Applications of the Random Walk).
explanation: The pointwise limit is not uniform in x: the telegraph solution vanishes identically for |x| > v t while the Gaussian does not, so the relative error is O(1) (indeed 100 percent) in the far tail no matter how large lambda t is.

premises: A random walker on a lattice of spacing a that steps to a random neighbour every tau seconds has, on scales x >> a and t >> tau, a coarse-grained density obeying dc/dt = D d^2c/dx^2 with D = a^2/(2 tau).
In a bench experiment the concentration of a dye in water is found, on millimetre and minute scales, to obey dc/dt = D d^2c/dx^2 with D = 1.0e-9 m^2/s to within measurement error.
conclusion: The dye molecules therefore move between collisions in steps of a fixed length a separated by a fixed time tau, with a^2 = 2 D tau.
source: Misconception that the macroscopic diffusion equation identifies the microscopic dynamics; discussed in Chandrasekhar (1943) and in van Kampen.
explanation: Coarse-graining runs one way: continuous-step walks, Langevin dynamics, persistent walks and many other microscopic models all give the same diffusion equation, so the macroscopic law cannot be inverted to recover a lattice step law.

premises: The free Schroedinger equation i hbar dpsi/dt = -(hbar^2/2m) d^2psi/dx^2 can be written as a diffusion equation dpsi/dt = D_q d^2psi/dx^2 with complex diffusivity D_q = i hbar/(2m), of magnitude hbar/(2m).
For the diffusion equation du/dt = D d^2u/dx^2 the variance of an initially localized packet grows linearly, <x^2>(t) = 2 D t.
conclusion: A free quantum wave packet therefore spreads diffusively, its position variance growing as <Delta x^2>(t) = hbar t/m.
source: Common misreading of the Schroedinger-diffusion correspondence; contrast with the exact free Gaussian packet result in any quantum mechanics text.
explanation: The shared PDE form is a mathematical analogy, not a physical equivalence: psi is not a probability density and the actual free packet obeys sigma^2(t) = sigma_0^2 + (hbar t/(2 m sigma_0))^2, quadratic rather than linear in t.

premises: A particle moving in one dimension has a stationary velocity process v(t) with autocorrelation C(t) = <v(0) v(t)>, satisfying C(-t) = C(t), and C decays fast enough that integral_0^infinity |C(t)| dt and integral_0^infinity t |C(t)| dt are both finite.
The displacement is x(t) - x(0) = integral_0^t v(t') dt', so that, by stationarity, <(x(t) - x(0))^2> = 2 integral_0^t (t - s) C(s) ds.
The diffusion coefficient is defined as D = lim_{t -> infinity} <(x(t) - x(0))^2> / (2 t).
conclusion: D = integral_0^infinity C(t) dt.
source: Green-Kubo relation for self-diffusion (Kubo 1957; Zwanzig, Nonequilibrium Statistical Mechanics, ch. 4).
explanation: Dividing the double-integral expression by 2t gives integral_0^t C(s) ds minus (1/t) integral_0^t s C(s) ds; the assumed integrability makes the second term vanish as t -> infinity, leaving the time integral of C.

premises: A particle of mass m obeys the Langevin equation m dv/dt = -gamma v + xi(t), where gamma > 0 is a friction coefficient with units kg/s.
xi(t) is Gaussian white noise with <xi(t)> = 0 and <xi(t) xi(t')> = 2 gamma k_B T delta(t - t').
At t = 0 the velocity is in thermal equilibrium, <v(0)^2> = k_B T / m, and v(0) is uncorrelated with xi(t) for all t > 0 (causality).
conclusion: <v(0) v(t)> = (k_B T / m) exp(-gamma t / m) for t >= 0.
source: Ornstein-Uhlenbeck velocity process (Uhlenbeck & Ornstein 1930; Reif, Fundamentals of Statistical and Thermal Physics, sec. 15.7).
explanation: Multiplying the formal solution v(t) = v(0) exp(-gamma t/m) + (1/m) integral_0^t exp(-gamma (t-s)/m) xi(s) ds by v(0) and averaging, the noise term drops out by causality, giving the exponential decay with the equilibrium prefactor.

premises: A passive solute of molecular diffusivity D is carried by steady Poiseuille flow in a straight circular tube of radius a, with axial velocity u(r) = 2 U (1 - r^2/a^2), where U is the cross-sectional mean speed.
The concentration c(r, z, t) obeys the advection-diffusion equation dc/dt + u(r) dc/dz = D (nabla_perp^2 c + d^2c/dz^2) with zero flux through the tube wall (partial derivatives understood).
The solute cloud is observed at times t >> a^2 / D, so that radial diffusion has mixed the solute across the section, and its axial extent is much larger than a.
conclusion: The cross-sectionally averaged concentration obeys a one-dimensional advection-diffusion equation in the frame moving with speed U, with effective axial diffusivity D_eff = D + a^2 U^2 / (48 D).
source: Taylor dispersion (Taylor, Proc. R. Soc. A 219, 186 (1953); Aris 1956 moment method).
explanation: Averaging over the cross-section and solving for the small radial concentration deviation in the long-time regime yields an enhanced axial diffusivity; the 1/48 coefficient is the classical Taylor-Aris result for a circular tube.

premises: An overdamped Brownian particle in one dimension obeys the Smoluchowski equation dp/dt = d/dx [ D0 ( dp/dx + (V'(x) / (k_B T)) p ) ] with a constant bare diffusivity D0 (partial derivatives understood).
The potential V(x) is smooth and periodic with period L, V(x + L) = V(x), and the bath is at temperature T.
Angle brackets <f> denote the spatial average (1/L) integral_0^L f(x) dx over one period.
conclusion: On length scales much larger than L and times much longer than L^2 / D0, the particle performs ordinary diffusion with effective coefficient D_eff = D0 / ( <exp(V / k_B T)> <exp(-V / k_B T)> ).
source: Lifson-Jackson formula (Lifson & Jackson, J. Chem. Phys. 36, 2410 (1962)); also derived by homogenization of the Smoluchowski equation.
explanation: Homogenization (or the mean first-passage time over one period) shows that the large-scale dynamics is free diffusion with D_eff given by the product of the two Boltzmann-factor averages, which reduces to D0 for a flat potential.

premises: An incompressible Newtonian fluid of kinematic viscosity nu fills the half-space y > 0 above a flat plate; at t = 0 the plate is impulsively set moving in its own plane at speed U_0. With no pressure gradient and a unidirectional velocity u = u(y, t), the Navier-Stokes equations reduce to du/dt = nu d^2u/dy^2 with u(0, t) = U_0, u(y, 0) = 0 and u -> 0 as y -> infinity.

A semi-infinite solid y > 0 of thermal diffusivity alpha, initially at uniform temperature T_i, has its surface held at T_s for t > 0. Its temperature obeys dT/dt = alpha d^2T/dy^2 and is given by (T - T_i) / (T_s - T_i) = erfc( y / (2 sqrt(alpha t)) ).
conclusion: The velocity profile has the same mathematical form as the temperature profile, with the kinematic viscosity in the role of the thermal diffusivity: u(y, t) / U_0 = erfc( y / (2 sqrt(nu t)) ).
source: Stokes' first (Rayleigh) problem, Schlichting, Boundary-Layer Theory; comparison with Carslaw & Jaeger semi-infinite solid.
explanation: Both problems are the same linear PDE with the same initial and boundary data after renaming (u/U_0 <-> (T - T_i)/(T_s - T_i), nu <-> alpha), so the solutions coincide in form, although one describes momentum transport by viscous stress and the other heat conduction.

premises: In a homogeneous half-space y > 0 the temperature obeys dT/dt = alpha d^2T/dy^2 with constant thermal diffusivity alpha.
For real wavenumber k, the equation admits solutions exp(i k y - i omega t) with complex frequency fixed by the dispersion relation omega = -i alpha k^2, i.e. pure exponential decay in time.
The surface temperature is driven periodically, T(0, t) = T_0 + Delta T cos(omega t) with real omega > 0, and the temperature must remain bounded as y -> infinity.
conclusion: Solving the same dispersion relation for complex k at real omega and keeping the branch that is bounded at large y, the temperature oscillation decays into the solid as exp(-y / delta) with penetration depth delta = sqrt(2 alpha / omega).
source: Periodic surface heating (Kelvin; Angstrom method); Carslaw & Jaeger, Conduction of Heat in Solids, sec. 2.6.
explanation: Continuing the dispersion relation from real k, complex omega to real omega, complex k gives k^2 = i omega / alpha, whose bounded root k = (1 + i) sqrt(omega / (2 alpha)) yields a damped thermal wave with equal decay length and inverse wavenumber delta.

premises: A quantum Brownian particle linearly coupled to an Ohmic bath with friction coefficient gamma experiences a fluctuating force whose symmetrized two-sided spectral density, S_F(omega) = integral_{-infinity}^{infinity} <{F(t), F(0)}/2> exp(i omega t) dt, is S_F(omega) = gamma hbar omega coth( hbar omega / (2 k_B T) ) (quantum fluctuation-dissipation theorem).
In the same two-sided convention, the classical Langevin force with <F(t) F(t')> = 2 gamma k_B T delta(t - t') has the flat spectrum 2 gamma k_B T.
Only frequencies satisfying hbar |omega| << k_B T are relevant to the dynamics considered.
conclusion: In this regime the quantum spectrum reduces to the classical white-noise spectrum, S_F(omega) = 2 gamma k_B T, with relative corrections of order (hbar omega / k_B T)^2.
source: Callen-Welton theorem and its classical (hbar -> 0) limit; Weiss, Quantum Dissipative Systems, ch. 3.
explanation: With x = hbar omega / (2 k_B T), x coth x = 1 + x^2/3 + O(x^4), so the quantum spectrum is 2 gamma k_B T times a factor that tends to 1 as hbar -> 0 at fixed omega and T; the classical Langevin noise is the hbar -> 0 limit of the quantum one.

premises: A one-dimensional diffusion process is defined by the Ito stochastic differential equation dx = a(x) dt + b(x) dW, with W a standard Wiener process and a, b smooth; its transition density obeys the Fokker-Planck equation dp/dt = -d(a p)/dx + (1/2) d^2(b^2 p)/dx^2.

A Stratonovich stochastic differential equation dx = A(x) dt + B(x) o dW, defined with the midpoint rule for the stochastic integral, has transition density obeying dp/dt = -d(A p)/dx + (1/2) d/dx [ B d(B p)/dx ].
The two equations are to have the same noise amplitude, B(x) = b(x).
conclusion: The Ito and Stratonovich equations describe exactly the same stochastic process (identical transition probabilities) if and only if their drifts are related by A(x) = a(x) - (1/2) b(x) b'(x).
source: Ito-Stratonovich drift correction; Gardiner, Handbook of Stochastic Methods, sec. 4.3.6; van Kampen 1981.
explanation: Expanding the Stratonovich Fokker-Planck operator gives -d((A + b b'/2) p)/dx + (1/2) d^2(b^2 p)/dx^2, which coincides with the Ito operator exactly when A = a - b b'/2; since the generator determines the Markov process, the two descriptions are the same physics in different stochastic calculi.

premises: A rigid sphere of radius a is suspended in an unbounded incompressible Newtonian fluid of shear viscosity eta at temperature T; the Reynolds number of its motion is negligible, so the surrounding flow is Stokes flow.
The mobility mu is defined through the steady drift velocity under a constant applied force, v = mu F, and the Einstein relation D = mu k_B T holds.
conclusion: The diffusion coefficient of the sphere is D = k_B T / (6 pi eta a).
source: Stokes-Einstein-Sutherland relation (Einstein 1905, Sutherland 1905); slip-dependence discussed in Lamb, Hydrodynamics, and Happel & Brenner.
explanation: The factor 6 pi eta a for the Stokes drag presupposes the no-slip (stick) boundary condition on the sphere surface, which the premises never state; with perfect slip the Stokes drag is 4 pi eta a v and the result becomes D = k_B T / (4 pi eta a).

premises: Fourier's law q = -k dT/dx relates the heat flux in a solid to the temperature gradient through the thermal conductivity k; combined with steady-state energy conservation dq/dx = 0 it gives a linear temperature profile across a slab.

A single-crystal silicon film of thickness L = 20 nm at 300 K is held between two reservoirs differing in temperature by Delta T. The bulk thermal conductivity of silicon at 300 K is k = 150 W/(m K), and the phonons carrying most of the heat at this temperature have mean free paths of order 300 nm.
Transport across the film is one-dimensional and steady.
conclusion: The steady heat flux through the film is q = (150 W/(m K)) Delta T / L.
source: Casimir (1938) boundary-scattering limit; G. Chen, Nanoscale Energy Transport and Conversion, ch. 7; measured thin-film silicon conductivities.
explanation: Fourier's law with the bulk conductivity is valid only when the sample dimension greatly exceeds the phonon mean free path; at L = 20 nm << 300 nm transport is quasi-ballistic, the effective conductivity is several times below the bulk value, and the linear-profile formula is applied outside its range.

premises: By the Nyquist-Johnson formula in the engineering convention, the thermal force on a Brownian particle with friction coefficient gamma has one-sided spectral density S_F(f) = 4 gamma k_B T, where f >= 0 is the frequency in Hz and <F^2> = integral_0^infinity S_F(f) df.

A stationary white noise with autocorrelation <F(t) F(t')> = Gamma delta(t - t') has two-sided spectral density S(omega) = integral_{-infinity}^{infinity} <F(t) F(0)> exp(i omega t) dt = Gamma, flat in omega, with <F^2> = integral_{-infinity}^{infinity} S(omega) domega / (2 pi).
For the overdamped Langevin equation gamma dx/dt = F(t) with <F(t) F(t')> = Gamma delta(t - t'), the diffusion coefficient is D = Gamma / (2 gamma^2).
conclusion: Identifying the flat white-noise spectrum with the Nyquist value gives the diffusion coefficient D = 2 k_B T / gamma.
source: Classic factor-of-two error between one-sided per-Hz and two-sided per-(rad/s) spectral densities; see Kittel, Elementary Statistical Physics, and errata to several noise chapters.
explanation: With these normalizations the one-sided density equals twice the two-sided one, S_F(f) = 2 S(omega), so the correct identification is Gamma = 2 gamma k_B T and D = k_B T / gamma; the claim sets Gamma = 4 gamma k_B T by mixing the two conventions.

premises: A particle in one dimension moves at constant speed v and reverses its direction at random instants forming a Poisson process; the mean time between successive reversals is tau.

The probability density of such a persistent random walk obeys the telegraph equation tau d^2p/dt^2 + dp/dt = D d^2p/dx^2, where tau is the relaxation time of the velocity autocorrelation <v(0) v(t)> = v^2 exp(-t / tau) and D = v^2 tau is the long-time diffusion coefficient (partial derivatives understood).
conclusion: The long-time diffusion coefficient of the persistent random walk is D = v^2 tau, where tau is the mean time between reversals.
source: Goldstein (1951) / Kac persistent random walk; the factor-of-two pitfall is discussed in Weiss, Aspects and Applications of the Random Walk.
explanation: The symbol tau denotes two different times: with mean reversal interval tau_r each reversal flips the sign of v, so the velocity autocorrelation is v^2 exp(-2 t / tau_r) and the telegraph relaxation time is tau_r / 2, giving D = v^2 tau_r / 2, half the claimed value.

premises: In a unidirectional flow of an incompressible Newtonian fluid, momentum diffuses according to du/dt = nu d^2u/dy^2, where nu = eta / rho is the kinematic viscosity with units m^2/s; for water at 20 °C, nu = 1.0e-6 m^2/s.
A dilute passive solute in the same fluid obeys Fick's second law dc/dt = D d^2c/dx^2, where D also has units m^2/s, and a solute molecule's mean squared displacement grows as <x^2> = 2 D t.

Both coefficients are transport coefficients of the same solvent, have the same dimensions m^2/s, and multiply the second spatial derivative in equations of identical form; the water is at rest at 20 °C.
conclusion: A sucrose molecule in this water therefore has mean squared displacement <x^2> = 2 (1.0e-6 m^2/s) t.
source: Common student conflation of momentum diffusivity with mass diffusivity; Bird, Stewart & Lightfoot on the Schmidt number of liquids.
explanation: Kinematic viscosity and mass diffusivity merely share units; they are different physical quantities set by different mechanisms, and for sucrose in water D is about 5e-10 m^2/s (Schmidt number nu/D of order 2000), not 1.0e-6 m^2/s.

premises: A Brownian particle of mass m and friction coefficient gamma obeys m dv/dt = -gamma v + xi(t) with <xi(t) xi(t')> = 2 gamma k_B T delta(t - t'), in equilibrium at temperature T.

In the limit m -> 0 at fixed gamma and T, the position process converges to the overdamped Langevin equation gamma dx/dt = xi(t), whose mean squared displacement is <(Delta x)^2> = 2 D t with D = k_B T / gamma for every t > 0.
For a micrometre-sized colloidal sphere in water the momentum relaxation time m / gamma is a few hundred nanoseconds, so m is negligibly small and the overdamped description is taken to apply.
conclusion: Hence the mean squared displacement of the colloidal sphere is linear at all times, with initial slope d<(Delta x)^2>/dt at t = 0 equal to 2 k_B T / gamma.
source: Ballistic Brownian motion (Uhlenbeck & Ornstein 1930; Li et al., Science 328, 1673 (2010)); textbook warning in Pathria & Beale on the short-time regime.
explanation: The m -> 0 limit is not uniform in t: for any finite m the exact result <(Delta x)^2> = 2 D [ t - (m/gamma)(1 - exp(-gamma t / m)) ] behaves as (k_B T / m) t^2 for t << m / gamma, so the slope at t = 0 is zero; the limits t -> 0 and m -> 0 do not commute.

premises: In a rigid isotropic solid with constant density rho and specific heat c, conservation of energy reads rho c dT/dt = -div q, where q is the heat flux vector.
Every temperature field measured in the solid is found to satisfy the heat equation dT/dt = alpha nabla^2 T with the same constant alpha.
Fourier's law q = -k grad T, inserted into the energy equation, implies the heat equation with alpha = k / (rho c).
conclusion: Therefore the heat flux in the solid is q = -rho c alpha grad T.
source: Non-uniqueness of the heat flux given only the temperature field; Day, Heat Conduction Within Linear Thermoelasticity; Truesdell on constitutive theory.
explanation: The heat equation only constrains div q; any flux of the form q = -k grad T + curl A(x, t) (a solenoidal circulating heat current) produces the identical temperature evolution, so the constitutive law cannot be recovered by running the derivation backwards from the temperature field.

premises: The free-particle Schrodinger equation i hbar dpsi/dt = -(hbar^2 / 2m) d^2psi/dx^2 can be rewritten as dpsi/dt = D_q d^2psi/dx^2 with the imaginary coefficient D_q = i hbar / (2m).
A diffusion equation dp/dt = D d^2p/dx^2 with real D > 0 describes a random walker whose mean squared displacement grows as <x^2> = 2 D t.
For the quantum particle the position variance is computed from |psi|^2, and the initial state is a real Gaussian wavepacket of width sigma_0 centred at x = 0.
conclusion: Because the Schrodinger equation is a diffusion equation with diffusion constant of magnitude hbar / (2m), the wavepacket spreads diffusively as <x^2>(t) = hbar t / m.
source: Misreading of the Wick-rotation correspondence between the heat kernel and the free propagator; standard wavepacket-spreading result in any quantum mechanics text (e.g. Griffiths, Problem 2.22).
explanation: The formal identity of the equations does not carry over to the observable, since |psi|^2 does not obey a diffusion equation; the exact result is <x^2>(t) = sigma_0^2 + (hbar t / (2 m sigma_0))^2, which is ballistic rather than diffusive at long times.

premises: A scalar field phi(x,t) obeys the one-dimensional Klein-Gordon equation (1/c^2) d^2phi/dt^2 - d^2phi/dx^2 + (m c/hbar)^2 phi = 0, with c the speed of light, m > 0 a constant mass and hbar the reduced Planck constant.
Plane-wave solutions phi = exp(i(kx - omega t)) with real k are substituted, giving omega^2 = c^2 k^2 + (m c^2/hbar)^2.
The phase velocity is defined as v_p = omega/k and the group velocity as v_g = d omega/dk, with k > 0 and the positive root omega > 0 taken.
conclusion: v_p v_g = c^2
source: Standard result for the Klein-Gordon dispersion relation; e.g. Bjorken and Drell, Relativistic Quantum Mechanics, ch. 9; also Crawford, Waves, ch. 4.
explanation: Differentiating omega^2 = c^2 k^2 + const gives v_g = c^2 k/omega, and multiplying by v_p = omega/k gives exactly c^2; the derivation is one-way and exact.

premises: A function u(x,t) is twice continuously differentiable and satisfies the one-dimensional wave equation d^2u/dt^2 = c^2 d^2u/dx^2 with constant c > 0 on the whole real line.
New independent variables are introduced by xi = x - c t and eta = x + c t; this map is linear and invertible with x = (xi + eta)/2 and t = (eta - xi)/(2c).
Derivatives transform by the chain rule: d/dx = d/dxi + d/deta and d/dt = -c d/dxi + c d/deta.
conclusion: d^2u/(dxi deta) = 0
source: d'Alembert's reduction to characteristic coordinates; e.g. Morse and Ingard, Theoretical Acoustics, sec. 4.1; Strauss, Partial Differential Equations, sec. 2.1.
explanation: Substituting the chain-rule expressions gives u_tt - c^2 u_xx = -4 c^2 u_{xi eta}, so the two equations are the same statement in different coordinates and each implies the other; the general solution f(xi) + g(eta) follows in either description.

premises: A uniform stiff string of linear mass density mu, tension T and bending stiffness EI (Young's modulus times second moment of area) has small transverse displacement y(x,t) obeying mu d^2y/dt^2 = T d^2y/dx^2 - EI d^4y/dx^4, valid for wavelengths long compared with the string's thickness.
For plane waves y = exp(i(kx - omega t)) with real k this gives the dispersion relation omega^2 = (T/mu) k^2 + (EI/mu) k^4.
The tension is now set to zero, T = 0, all other parameters being unchanged.
conclusion: omega = sqrt(EI/mu) k^2
source: Euler-Bernoulli beam as the zero-tension case of the stiff string; e.g. Fletcher and Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, secs. 2.18-2.19; Morse and Ingard, sec. 5.1.
explanation: Imposing the extra condition T = 0 removes the k^2 term and leaves the free-beam relation omega^2 = (EI/mu) k^4 with omega > 0; this is a special case of the premise theory, not an approximation.

premises: In an ideal gas of molar mass M and adiabatic index gamma, sound propagates adiabatically with speed c = sqrt(gamma R T/M), where T is the absolute temperature in kelvin and R = 8.314 J/(mol K).
For dry air, gamma and M are taken constant over the range considered, and the speed at T = 273.15 K is c_0 = 331.3 m/s.
The Celsius temperature T_C is defined by T = 273.15 K + T_C, and the regime |T_C| <= 40 is considered.
source: Linearized temperature dependence of the speed of sound in air; e.g. Kinsler, Frey, Coppens and Sanders, Fundamentals of Acoustics, sec. 5.6; Halliday and Resnick, ch. 17.
explanation: c = c_0 sqrt(1 + T_C/273.15) is expanded to first order in T_C/273.15, giving slope c_0/(2 x 273.15) = 0.606 m/(s degC); the neglected term is at most (1/8)(40/273.15)^2 = 0.27 percent of c_0 in the stated range.

premises: A massless string under tension T carries point masses m at equal spacing a; the transverse displacement y_j of mass j obeys m d^2y_j/dt^2 = (T/a)(y_{j+1} - 2 y_j + y_{j-1}) for small displacements.
Normal modes y_j = exp(i(k j a - omega t)) have the exact dispersion relation omega = 2 sqrt(T/(m a)) |sin(k a/2)|.

Only disturbances whose wavelength is much larger than the spacing, k a << 1, are considered, and a smooth field y(x,t) is defined so that y(j a, t) = y_j(t) with mu = m/a the average mass per unit length.
conclusion: d^2y/dt^2 = (T a/m) d^2y/dx^2
source: Continuum limit of the beaded string / monatomic chain; e.g. French, Vibrations and Waves, ch. 5; Crawford, Waves, sec. 2.4.
explanation: Replacing the second difference by a a^2 d^2y/dx^2 when the field varies slowly over many spacings gives the string wave equation with speed sqrt(T/mu) = sqrt(T a/m); this is the large-scale description of the discrete lattice and discards the k a ~ 1 behaviour.

premises: A stretched string resting on a uniform elastic foundation (restoring force per unit length -kappa_f y) obeys d^2y/dt^2 = c^2 d^2y/dx^2 - omega_0^2 y with c^2 = T/mu and omega_0^2 = kappa_f/mu, both constant.
For real wavenumber k the dispersion relation is omega^2 = c^2 k^2 + omega_0^2, so propagating solutions exist only for omega >= omega_0.

The string is driven at one end at a fixed angular frequency omega < omega_0, and the steady-state solution y = Y(x) exp(-i omega t) is sought in the form Y = exp(i k x) with k now allowed to be complex, k = i kappa with kappa > 0 chosen so that Y is bounded as x -> +infinity.
conclusion: kappa = sqrt(omega_0^2 - omega^2)/c
source: Evanescent waves below cutoff in a Klein-Gordon-type medium; e.g. Crawford, Waves, sec. 3.5; Morse and Ingard, sec. 4.1.
explanation: Substituting k = i kappa into the same equation gives omega^2 = -c^2 kappa^2 + omega_0^2, which is the dispersion relation continued to imaginary wavenumber; the bounded root gives the stated decay constant.

premises: In a hollow perfectly conducting waveguide of uniform cross-section, a TE mode has fields proportional to exp(i(k z - omega t)) times a transverse profile, and Maxwell's equations in vacuum give omega^2 = c^2 k^2 + omega_c^2, where omega_c is the mode's cutoff frequency fixed by the cross-section geometry and c is the speed of light.
A free relativistic scalar particle of mass m is described by the Klein-Gordon equation, whose plane waves obey omega^2 = c^2 k^2 + (m c^2/hbar)^2.
The two systems are otherwise unrelated: the waveguide relation involves no Planck constant and no particle mass, and its cutoff can be changed by changing the guide dimensions.
conclusion: omega^2 = c^2 k^2 + omega_c^2
source: Waveguide dispersion as a classical analogue of the Klein-Gordon relation; e.g. Jackson, Classical Electrodynamics, sec. 8.3; Crawford, Waves, ch. 4 (discussion of cutoff).
explanation: The two dispersion relations have identical mathematical form with omega_c playing the role of m c^2/hbar, so results such as v_p v_g = c^2 transfer, but the claim is only that the forms coincide; no physical identification of a photon mass is made.

premises: A complex scalar field psi(x,t) obeys the Klein-Gordon equation -hbar^2 d^2psi/dt^2 = -hbar^2 c^2 Laplacian psi + m^2 c^4 psi.

The field is written in eikonal form psi = A(x,t) exp(i S(x,t)/hbar) with real A and S, and S is held fixed while hbar -> 0 is taken; terms of order hbar^1 and hbar^2 relative to the leading term are dropped.
S is identified with Hamilton's principal function of a classical particle, so that E = -dS/dt and p = grad S.
conclusion: (dS/dt)^2 - c^2 (grad S)^2 = m^2 c^4
source: Classical (WKB/eikonal) limit of the Klein-Gordon equation giving the relativistic Hamilton-Jacobi equation; e.g. Landau and Lifshitz, Classical Theory of Fields, sec. 16; Bjorken and Drell, ch. 9.
explanation: At leading order in hbar the substitution yields exactly the relativistic Hamilton-Jacobi equation E^2 = p^2 c^2 + m^2 c^4, showing the Klein-Gordon equation is the quantum deformation whose hbar -> 0 limit is the classical relativistic particle.

premises: A linear, homogeneous, time-invariant medium supports plane waves exp(i(kx - omega t)) with a dispersion relation omega = omega(k), and the group velocity is v_g = d omega/dk.
A narrow-band wave packet centred at k_0 carries a time-averaged energy density <w> and a time-averaged energy flux <S>, and the energy transport velocity is defined by v_E = <S>/<w>.
Energy conservation holds in the form dw/dt + dS/dx = 0 for the fields of the medium.
conclusion: v_E = d omega/dk evaluated at k = k_0
source: Brillouin, Wave Propagation and Group Velocity (1960); Landau and Lifshitz, Electrodynamics of Continuous Media, sec. 84, where the equality is shown to require a transparent (non-absorbing) medium.
explanation: The equality of energy velocity and group velocity holds only when the medium is lossless (real dispersion relation, no absorption); the premises never state that the medium is non-dissipative, and in absorbing media near resonance v_g and v_E differ and v_g may even exceed c or be negative.

premises: A stiff string with hinged ends of length L, tension T, linear density mu and bending stiffness EI has partial frequencies f_n given by the dispersion relation omega^2 = (T/mu) k^2 + (EI/mu) k^4 with k_n = n pi/L.
With the inharmonicity parameter B = pi^2 EI/(T L^2) and fundamental f_1 = (1/2L) sqrt(T/mu), the partials satisfy f_n = n f_1 (1 + B n^2/2) to first order in the small stiffness parameter B.
A piano bass string has B = 1.0 x 10^-4, and the frequency of its 200th partial is required.
source: Stiff-string inharmonicity formula (Fletcher and Rossing, sec. 2.18; Morse and Ingard sec. 5.1); the expansion parameter is B n^2, a point often lost when B alone is quoted as small.
explanation: The first-order formula is an expansion in B n^2, not in B; at n = 200 one has B n^2 = 4, far outside the regime of validity, and the hinged-end relation gives f_200 = 200 f_1 sqrt(1 + 4) = 447 f_1, not 600 f_1.

premises: A relativistic field-theory text with metric signature (+,-,-,-) writes the free Klein-Gordon equation as (box + mu^2) phi = 0, where box = d_mu d^mu = (1/c^2) d^2/dt^2 - Laplacian and mu = m c/hbar.
A general-relativity text with metric signature (-,+,+,+) writes the same physical equation as (box - mu^2) phi = 0, where its box is g^{mu nu} d_mu d_nu.
Plane waves phi = exp(i(k.x - omega t)) with real k are substituted into the equation (box - mu^2) phi = 0 using box = (1/c^2) d^2/dt^2 - Laplacian.
conclusion: omega^2 = c^2 k^2 - (m c^2/hbar)^2
source: Metric-signature sign errors in the Klein-Gordon operator; a well-known pitfall discussed e.g. in Peskin and Schroeder ch. 2 (note on conventions) and in errata to several GR/QFT texts.
explanation: The operator box changes overall sign between the two signatures, so (box - mu^2) from the (-,+,+,+) text must be paired with box = -(1/c^2) d_t^2 + Laplacian; combining the (-,+,+,+) equation with the (+,-,-,-) operator flips the sign of the mass term and produces a spurious tachyonic dispersion relation instead of omega^2 = c^2 k^2 + (m c^2/hbar)^2.

premises: A sinusoidal transverse wave travels along a uniform stretched string of linear mass density mu; its period is T and its wavelength is lambda, so the wave speed is v = lambda / T.
Transverse waves on a string under tension T travel at speed v = sqrt(T/mu), for small-amplitude displacements.
Equating the two expressions for v and solving for lambda gives lambda = T v.
conclusion: lambda = T^(3/2) / sqrt(mu)
source: Classic student error with the symbol T used for both period and tension in string-wave problems; noted in instructor commentaries to Halliday/Resnick ch. 16 and Serway ch. 16.
explanation: The symbol T denotes the period (seconds) in the first premise and the tension (newtons) in the second; the derivation treats them as the same quantity, and the resulting expression is dimensionally meaningless (the correct result is lambda = T_period sqrt(T_tension/mu)).

premises: Plane-wave solutions of the Klein-Gordon equation for a particle of mass m > 0 obey omega^2 = c^2 k^2 + (m c^2/hbar)^2, with c the speed of light.
The phase velocity of a plane wave is omega/k, and for these waves omega/k = c sqrt(1 + (m c/(hbar k))^2), which exceeds c for every finite real k.
A signal is any disturbance of the field that propagates through space, and its speed is a velocity measured in metres per second.
conclusion: v_signal = c sqrt(1 + (m c/(hbar k))^2)
source: Well-known misconception that the superluminal phase velocity of de Broglie/Klein-Gordon waves is a signal velocity; addressed in Brillouin (1960) and in Crawford, Waves, ch. 6.
explanation: Phase velocity and signal (front) velocity are both measured in m/s but are different physical quantities; the phase velocity of an infinite monochromatic wave carries no information, and the front velocity of a Klein-Gordon disturbance is exactly c, with v_g = c^2 k/omega < c.

premises: A string of length L with fixed ends carries N equally spaced beads of mass m at spacing a = L/(N+1), and the massless string between them is under tension T; the exact normal-mode frequencies are f_n = (1/pi) sqrt(T/(m a)) sin(n pi/(2(N+1))) for n = 1, ..., N.
In the continuum limit N -> infinity at fixed L and fixed mu = m/a, the beaded string becomes a uniform string with wave speed v = sqrt(T/mu), whose modes are f_n = n v/(2L).
For a piano-like string modelled with N = 1000 beads, the highest mode n = N is considered, and N is large enough that the continuum limit applies.
conclusion: f_N = N v/(2L)
source: Non-uniform convergence of the discrete-chain spectrum to the string spectrum; discussed in French, Vibrations and Waves, ch. 5 and in Crawford, Waves, sec. 2.4 (dispersion near the zone boundary).
explanation: The limit f_n -> n v/(2L) holds for each fixed n as N -> infinity but not uniformly in n; for n = N the sine saturates and f_N -> v/(pi a) while N v/(2L) -> v/(2a), so the ratio is 2/pi and the continuum formula is wrong for the highest modes no matter how large N is.

premises: In a medium whose dispersion relation is omega = c k with constant c, every disturbance u(x,t) = f(x - c t) propagates without change of shape at speed c, since d'Alembert's solution applies.
A localized transverse pulse on a long stretched cable resting on a stiff nonlinear foundation is observed to travel several hundred metres at constant speed c_s with no measurable change of shape.
The medium is homogeneous and time-invariant, so it admits a well-defined dispersion relation for small-amplitude sinusoidal waves.
conclusion: omega = c_s k
source: Converse of the nondispersive-propagation theorem; solitary waves in dispersive nonlinear media (Russell 1834; Korteweg-de Vries 1895) are the standard counterexample.
explanation: Nondispersion implies shape preservation, but the converse is a one-way relation run backwards: a shape-preserving pulse can be a soliton in which nonlinearity balances dispersion, so the small-amplitude dispersion relation need not be linear in k.

premises: Small transverse displacements y(x,t) of a uniform string of tension T and linear density mu obey d^2y/dt^2 = c^2 d^2y/dx^2 with c = sqrt(T/mu), in the rest frame of the string.

This equation is form-invariant under the Lorentz transformation x' = gamma (x - V t), t' = gamma (t - V x/c^2), gamma = 1/sqrt(1 - V^2/c^2), with c = sqrt(T/mu) as the invariant speed, exactly as the electromagnetic wave equation is invariant with the speed of light.
An observer moves along the string at constant speed V < c relative to the string and measures the speed of a transverse pulse.
conclusion: c' = c
source: Misapplication of the Lorentz invariance of the wave equation to a medium-supported wave; discussed as a warning in French, Special Relativity, ch. 2 and in Feynman Lectures vol. I ch. 15 (ether analogy).
explanation: The mathematical invariance of the string equation under a Lorentz-type map with parameter sqrt(T/mu) is only a formal analogy; the string is a material medium with a preferred rest frame, physical observers are related by Galilean transformations, and the moving observer measures pulse speeds c - V and c + V.

premises: Two uniform strings of linear densities mu_1 (x < 0) and mu_2 (x > 0) are joined at x = 0 by a massless knot and carry the same static tension T; small transverse displacements obey mu_i u_tt = T u_xx on each side.
A sinusoidal wave of angular frequency omega is incident from x < 0; the displacement u and the slope u_x are continuous at x = 0 (the knot has no mass, so the transverse forces on it balance).
The characteristic impedance of each string is defined as Z_i = sqrt(T mu_i), so that the wavenumbers are k_i = omega Z_i / T.
conclusion: The amplitude reflection coefficient for the displacement, referred to the incident amplitude, is r = (Z_1 - Z_2)/(Z_1 + Z_2).
source: Standard string-junction problem (French, Vibrations and Waves; Crawford, Waves).
explanation: Writing incident, reflected and transmitted waves and imposing continuity of u and u_x at x = 0 gives 1 + r = t and k_1(1 - r) = k_2 t, whence r = (k_1 - k_2)/(k_1 + k_2) = (Z_1 - Z_2)/(Z_1 + Z_2).

premises: A twice continuously differentiable field u(x,t) on the whole line satisfies the one-dimensional wave equation u_tt = c^2 u_xx with constant c > 0.
Define the characteristic (Riemann) variables r = u_t + c u_x and s = u_t - c u_x.
conclusion: The wave equation is equivalent to a pair of decoupled first-order advection equations for r and s, the right-moving one being r_t - c r_x = 0, while s obeys the mirror equation with c replaced by -c; conversely, from any smooth (r, s) obeying these two equations one recovers a solution u of the wave equation, unique up to a constant.
source: Characteristic form of the 1D wave equation (Whitham, Linear and Nonlinear Waves; Strauss, PDE).
explanation: Direct differentiation gives r_t - c r_x = u_tt - c^2 u_xx = 0 and s_t + c s_x = 0; conversely the two advection equations are exactly the integrability condition for u_t = (r+s)/2, u_x = (r-s)/(2c), and then u_tt = c^2 u_xx follows, so each description implies the other.
